title: Can I request a menu tasting before booking catering in Dubai?
body_markdown:
Yes—you can request a catering menu tasting in Dubai before booking, but the request does not guarantee a session or make it part of the quotation. Ask whether a tasting is offered for your event, which dishes it covers and what terms apply. Get those details in writing before treating the tasting as a step towards confirming your caterer.


**TL;DR**

- For a catering menu tasting Dubai enquiry, ask about the dishes, format and terms before confirming attendance.
- A tasting helps assess food; it does not prove how the full event will run.
- Ask to sample dietary alternatives alongside the main menu, not after approving it.
- myCHEF provides Dubai catering; request tasting arrangements separately rather than assuming they are included.


## Can I request a menu tasting before booking catering in Dubai?

Yes. Make the request while discussing your event brief, before you approve the final menu or commit to a booking. The useful question is not simply whether you can taste the food. It is **whether the proposed tasting will help you decide on the actual event menu**.

Use this sequence:

1. **Send the event brief.** Include the date, venue, guest count, service format and dietary requirements.
2. **Ask about tasting arrangements.** Establish whether a session can be arranged before booking and what conditions apply.
3. **Agree on the dishes.** Identify the menu decisions you need the tasting to resolve.
4. **Confirm the next step.** Ask how feedback becomes a revised menu and when you must approve it.

If you are still choosing the service format, the [guest-list-to-plated-dinner planning guide](https://www.mychef.ae/blog/guest-list-to-plated-dinner-private-chef-event-workflow) covers the wider sequence. This article focuses on evaluating a menu before committing to it.

## Why does a tasting matter before you book?

A written menu cannot tell you whether you prefer a lighter sauce, a different spice level or a less sweet dessert. A tasting gives you something specific to discuss rather than relying on dish names and photographs.

It also has limits. Food served immediately to a small tasting group does not demonstrate delivery, buffet replenishment or coordinated service for your full guest list. **Approve the food and the event arrangements as separate decisions.**

For Dubai venues, include practical questions about loading access, kitchen facilities and outdoor service where relevant. Those details belong in the catering brief even when the tasting takes place elsewhere.

## What should you confirm before attending?

Ask for a short written outline of the session. It should distinguish what you will taste from what you will ultimately receive at the event.

### Which dishes will you try?

Request the exact dish names and identify any items that will not be sampled. A selection from a general menu is not the same as a tasting of your proposed menu.

Focus on unresolved choices. If your main concern is a vegetarian main course, a session centred on meat dishes will not answer it.

### What are the tasting terms?

Ask whether a tasting fee applies, what it covers and whether any amount is credited towards a confirmed event. Request the cancellation and rescheduling terms as well.

Do not assume that arranging a tasting reserves your event date. Ask what action confirms the booking and whether the tasting creates any obligation to proceed.

### Who should attend?

Choose people who can approve the menu and represent the guests' requirements. Agree who makes the final decision before collecting conflicting preferences around the table.

If a planner, venue coordinator or family member will approve changes, include that person in the feedback process. Confirm permitted attendance with the caterer rather than inviting additional guests without agreement.

## Which tasting format should you request?

Ask what formats the caterer can offer; do not assume every option is available. The right request depends on the decision you need to make.

| Format to ask about | Best for | What it helps assess | Main limitation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Proposed-menu tasting | Hosts close to approving their event menu | Specific dishes, balance and presentation | Does not demonstrate full-event delivery |
| Selected-dish tasting | Hosts deciding between particular dishes | Direct comparison of unresolved choices | Leaves the rest of the menu untested |
| Delivered samples | Hosts assessing a drop-off menu | Packaging, unpacking and condition on arrival | Does not show staffed service |
| Revised-dish tasting | Hosts resolving an important menu change | Whether the requested adjustment works | Requires separate agreement on arrangements |

**Match the tasting format to the service you intend to book.** Delivered food is best assessed with its delivery instructions and packaging. A plated dinner needs a separate conversation about finishing, serving and clearing each course.

A tasting need not recreate the whole celebration. It should answer a defined set of questions well enough for you to approve the next version of the proposal.

## How should you assess the food?

Start with your event brief, not a search for the most impressive individual dish. A menu needs to suit the guests, the occasion and the way food will be served.

Use these headings for your notes:

- **Flavour:** seasoning, spice, sweetness and the balance of sauces.
- **Texture:** tenderness, crispness and the contrast between components.
- **Portion:** whether the sample represents the intended event serving.
- **Presentation:** appearance and suitability for the chosen service format.
- **Dietary suitability:** ingredients, substitutions and questions requiring confirmation.


![Menu assessment checklist covering flavour, texture, portion, presentation and dietary suitability](https://gwvckixiegkllthleuyt.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/workspace-article-images-public/ec9886ec-cea0-49bb-b3f5-6519f51c8bac/body-4c6dc764af30d38600f7cfe79bf81df6.jpg)

*Assess each dish against the event brief, not appearance alone.*


Write observations that a chef can act on. Instead of saying a dish is wrong, identify the change: less sweetness, a milder sauce or a different accompaniment.

Also assess the menu as a whole. Several rich dishes can satisfy individually while leaving you wanting a fresher contrast across the meal. Ask how the proposed courses or buffet dishes work together.

## What should you ask about dietary requirements?

Send dietary requirements before the tasting menu is agreed. Separate allergies, intolerances, religious requirements and preferences so the caterer knows what needs clarification.

Ask for the relevant alternative to be included in the tasting discussion. Approving the main menu does not resolve whether a guest's separate meal will feel equally considered.

For allergies, ask directly about ingredients, preparation, shared equipment and service arrangements. **A tasting is not evidence that allergen controls have been agreed.** Obtain a clear response about what the caterer can accommodate before making a decision.

If halal suitability matters to your event, ask for confirmation for the specific dishes and ingredients. Do not infer suitability from the cuisine name or from a general description of the menu.

## Why do tasting arrangements vary?

The scope of your request changes what you need to confirm. These are the main factors to discuss:

- **Menu scope:** selected samples and a complete proposed menu answer different questions.
- **Service format:** plated dining, buffets and drop-off food require different practical checks.
- **Dietary requirements:** substitutions need their own ingredient and preparation discussion.
- **Venue facilities:** equipment and preparation space affect the event plan being evaluated.
- **Decision stage:** an exploratory enquiry needs a different brief from a final menu approval.
- **Requested revisions:** substantial changes require agreement on how they will be reviewed.

Ask the caterer to explain the proposed tasting in relation to your brief. A longer session is not automatically more useful; relevance matters more than the amount of food presented.

## Can a tasting show how the catering will work at the venue?

Only partly. A tasting can help you judge a dish, but you still need a delivery and service plan for the actual location.

For a villa or apartment event, establish access arrangements, preparation space and the equipment the caterer expects to use. For an office or hired venue, ask who approves access and who supplies the serving area.

For outdoor service, discuss how the setup and menu will respond to the conditions at the venue. Ask about the alternative plan rather than assuming an indoor tasting represents outdoor service.

Clarify responsibility for service staff, tableware, buffet equipment, clearing and kitchen handover. Record inclusions and exclusions in the proposal; a well-presented tasting table does not establish what comes with the event booking.

## What if you cannot arrange a tasting?

Ask for a detailed menu discussion and a written proposal that answers the same unresolved questions. Request ingredient descriptions, portion explanations, service arrangements and clear photographs where these are provided.

This is an alternative way to review the proposal, not an equivalent sensory test. You can clarify what a dish contains without learning exactly how it tastes.

Decide which uncertainties you can accept. If approving a particular dish depends on tasting it, say so before committing rather than expecting an additional session after booking.

## How do you turn tasting feedback into an approved menu?

Send one consolidated response after the session. Separate confirmed dishes from requested changes and questions that remain unanswered.

A useful feedback record includes:

- The dish name and the version you tasted.
- The elements you approve.
- The precise adjustment you request.
- Whether you need further clarification or another sample.
- Who will approve the revised menu.

Then request an updated proposal. Check that dish names, dietary alternatives, service format, responsibilities and exclusions match the agreement.

**A successful tasting ends with a clearer written menu, not just a favourable impression.** Do not leave an important change in a conversation that the final proposal does not reflect.

## What should you include in your first enquiry?

Give the caterer enough information to judge the request. A vague request to try some food leaves the purpose of the session unclear.

You can adapt this sample message:

*We are planning an event in Dubai on [date], at [location], for [guest count]. We are considering [service format] and would like to discuss a tasting before confirming the catering. Our priorities are [menu preferences], and our dietary requirements are [details]. Please explain the tasting arrangements, the dishes covered, the terms and how feedback is incorporated into the final proposal.*

Replace each bracketed detail before sending. Attach any venue requirements you already have, and identify the person authorised to approve the menu.

myCHEF provides catering for households and businesses in Dubai, with vetted chefs. A tasting request should form part of your event enquiry rather than be treated as a confirmed inclusion.

## FAQ


**Can I ask for a catering tasting before paying a booking deposit?**

Yes, you can ask for a tasting before paying a booking deposit. Confirm whether the caterer offers that arrangement and whether separate tasting terms apply before committing.

**Does a menu tasting reserve my event date?**

Do not treat a menu tasting as a date reservation unless the caterer confirms it in writing. Ask what action formally secures the booking.

**Can I choose which dishes to taste?**

Request the dishes that will help you resolve your menu decisions. Confirm the agreed selection in advance, including any dietary alternatives you need to assess.

**Should I taste every dish on my catering menu?**

Prioritise dishes where tasting will affect your decision rather than assuming you need to sample everything. Ask which parts of the proposed menu the session will leave untested.

**Can I request changes after the tasting?**

Yes, you can request changes after the tasting, but agree how revisions will be handled. Ask for an updated written menu and clarification of any effect on the proposal.

**Can a tasting confirm that food is suitable for an allergy?**

No, tasting food does not confirm allergy suitability. Ask separately about ingredients, preparation, shared equipment and service controls, and obtain a clear response before approving the menu.

**Does myCHEF guarantee a tasting before booking?**

Do not assume a tasting is guaranteed or included in a myCHEF catering enquiry. Request arrangements for your specific event and obtain confirmation before making plans around a session.

## Start with the decision you need to make

Before requesting a tasting, write down what would make you approve or reject the proposed menu. Share that with the caterer. It gives the session a purpose and makes feedback easier to resolve.

For a tailored myCHEF catering enquiry, send your **date, location, guest count and service required**, together with your menu preferences and dietary requirements. Ask whether a pre-booking tasting can be arranged and what it would cover.
